Mini Scissor Lift

A hand-cranked, screw-driven scissor lift designed for 3D printing. Eight parts, a 64 to 127 mm lifting stroke, and a design load of 9 kg, sized with a kinematics and statics model.

Specifications

Platform height64.0 mm collapsed, 126.9 mm extended
Stroke / height ratio62.9 mm / 1.98x
Links120 mm pin to pin, 12 x 4 mm, 4 mm pins, 2 link pairs
Lead screwM3 x 0.5 mm pitch, 52.8 mm travel, 105.5 turns
Design load9.0 kg, evenly distributed
Peak screw force242.6 N (collapsed)
Peak raising torque68.6 N·mm
Minimum safety factor2.01

Simulation results

The lift is hardest to raise when it is collapsed, because the links are nearly flat and the screw must push sideways against almost the full load. Screw force falls from 243 N to about 51 N as the lift rises, and the safety factor climbs from 2.0 to over 4.

How it was calculated

1. Kinematics

Slider position s = L·cos θ and height h = L·sin θ, so one knob turn moves the slider 0.5 mm and the height changes fastest at low angles.

2. Statics

Each link is solved as a free body with six pin reactions. The result matches the closed form below, with a maximum difference of 0.0 N.

3. Strength

Stress is checked at the net section through a pin hole (bending plus axial) and as pin bearing, against 35 MPa for printed PLA.

F_screw = W / tan θ  ·  T = F · (dm/2) · (l + π·μ·dm) / (π·dm − μ·l)

Assumptions: PLA yield 35 MPa, pin friction neglected, rigid platform, thread friction μ = 0.15, M3 pitch diameter 2.675 mm. Buckling and print-layer weakness are not modelled, and no physical testing was done. The CAD was generated with CadQuery and the analysis written in Python, with AI assistance.
